summary:
Ghosts of Space is an interactive website that helps young learners discover the stories behind spacecraft and equipment NASA left on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Through 13 illustrated mission stories based on NASA sources, learners explore why each mission was launched, what it discovered, and what remains after it ended.

Each story combines archival images, narrated text, interactive 3D models, and a short Mission Detective quiz. Mini-games bring mission challenges to life by letting learners try landing Mars Pathfinder, flying Ingenuity, or spotting a planet using the same principle as Kepler.

The project answers the challenge by showing how retired spacecraft continue to shape what we know. By connecting the equipment left behind to the discoveries it made possible, Ghosts of Space gives kids a way to explore space history at their own pace and see how one mission can lay the groundwork for the next.
details:
Ghosts of Space is an interactive website built in Bahrain to help young learners explore what NASA’s retired spacecraft and equipment left behind. The Mission Explorer brings together 13 stories from the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Each story follows a mission from its original purpose to what it discovered, what happened to the equipment, and how the science it made possible continues to be used.

Learners can read at their own pace or listen to a narrated version that highlights the current paragraph. They can start the audio at a specific passage, rotate and zoom in on 3D models, and step through mission diagrams. Each story ends with a four-question Mission Detective quiz that gives hints and explains the answers. The site also includes eight mini-games inspired by real missions. For example, in Land Pathfinder, players steer toward a landing zone and slow down before touchdown. Featured games link directly to their mission stories, so playing can be a starting point for learning.

We built the site with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The games use HTML Canvas, and the interactive 3D viewer uses the model-viewer library. We used NASA mission records and imagery as source material and linked to the original sources from the stories. We label simplified teaching models and use games to illustrate mission concepts. The site runs in a web browser and supports keyboard and touch controls.

We considered how children would discover a story, follow it independently, and check what they understood. That shaped the short narrated versions, replayable games, and quiz hints. Our intended impact is to make space history easier for children to explore at home or in class and to help them connect the equipment left behind with the observations that still inform science.
